Name: ptcg_agent_evolution
Title: Evolving a Pokémon TCG Battle Agent via Option-Scoring Policy Search in the cabt Simulator
Short Hypothesis: A heuristic option-scoring policy for the Pokémon Trading Card Game — covering lethal-attack detection, energy-attachment planning, bench development, and context-aware card selection — can be systematically improved through iterative search to substantially raise winrate against fixed baseline opponents in the cabt simulator, and card-database-informed lookahead yields further gains over purely reactive scoring.
Related Work: Game-playing agents for imperfect-information card games (Poker CFR lines, Hearthstone/MTG heuristic+search agents, RL for Pokémon TCG Live) typically combine hand-crafted evaluation with search or learned values. This task instantiates that program inside the cabt engine (the Kaggle 'pokemon-tcg-ai-battle' competition simulator, shipped with pip kaggle-environments): agents receive an observation with the full visible board state and a list of LEGAL options each decision, and return indices of chosen options. Unlike prior work requiring rules engines to be built, cabt provides perfect legality, so all research effort concentrates on decision quality — scoring, planning, and hidden-information reasoning.
Abstract: The Pokémon Trading Card Game is a two-player, imperfect-information card game combining resource management (energy attachment), tempo (a race to take 6 prize cards by knocking out opposing Pokémon), and combinatorial card effects. We study policy improvement for a PTCG agent in the cabt simulator available via `from kaggle_environments import make; env = make('cabt')`. Each decision, the engine hands the agent obs['select'] with a list of legal options (typed: main actions PLAY/ATTACH/EVOLVE/ABILITY/ATTACK/RETREAT/END, card picks with area/index, yes-no, counts) plus full visible state in obs['current'] (both players' boards, own hand, prize/deck counts) and obs['logs']; the agent returns a list of option indices (up to maxCount). The first call (obs['select'] is None) must return a fixed legal 60-card deck (provided). We start from a working baseline heuristic (provided in the seed code, ~90% winrate vs the built-in 'random' opponent, ~50% vs the stronger built-in 'first' opponent) and iteratively improve the option-scoring policy, evaluated by winrate over seat-alternated game batches against both baselines. The engine also exposes a complete card/attack database via the provided ctypes bindings (AllCard/AllAttack), enabling effect-aware play and lookahead. The goal is to maximize mean winrate across the two opponents (treated as two evaluation datasets: 'vs_random' and 'vs_first').
Experiments: E1 (baseline reproduction): Run the provided seed agent against BOTH built-in opponents 'random' and 'first' in cabt. Use at least 80 seat-alternated games per opponent (agent plays seat 0 in even games, seat 1 in odd games; win iff env.state[seat].reward == 1). Treat each opponent as a separate dataset named 'vs_random' and 'vs_first'. Record per-game outcomes and cumulative winrate curves. The single scalar evaluation metric for a run is mean_winrate = (winrate_vs_random + winrate_vs_first) / 2 — higher is better. Save all results into working/experiment_data.npy via np.save as a dict {dataset_name: {'wins': list, 'winrate_curve': list, 'final_winrate': float}, 'mean_winrate': float}, and save matplotlib figures (winrate curves per opponent, final winrate bar chart) as .png files in the working directory.

E2 (policy improvement): Improve the option-scoring policy in measurable increments: (a) lethal-attack detection also accounting for weakness (2x damage) and resistance (-30) from the card database via the pokemonType/weakness/resistance fields; (b) energy-attachment planning: attach toward the exact attack costs (attack 'energies' lists) of the intended attacker instead of always the active Pokémon; (c) bench development: keep 2-3 benched basics as backup attackers and evolve them when possible; (d) context-aware picks: heal the most-damaged own Pokémon, discard the least valuable card, target the opponent Pokémon closest to knockout for damage effects; (e) YES/NO and COUNT decisions tuned per context code. Re-run the E1 evaluation after each increment and report the winrate delta attributable to each change.

E3 (lookahead and card-effect awareness): Use the provided AllCard/AllAttack ctypes card database to (a) rank attacks by expected effective damage including weakness/resistance and (b) implement a 1-ply lookahead that checks whether the opponent's active Pokémon can knock out our attacker next turn (from its visible attacks and energy), preferring lines that take a prize without giving one back. Compare vs the best E2 policy on the E1 evaluation.

E4 (ablation): Starting from the best policy found, disable one component at a time (lethal detection, energy planning, bench development, lookahead) and measure the winrate drop on both datasets, quantifying each component's contribution.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Winrate estimates over small game counts are noisy (binomial std ~5.5% at 80 games); conclusions about small policy deltas require either more games or consistent direction across both opponents.
The built-in 'random' and 'first' opponents are weak, scripted baselines; winrate against them may overestimate strength against diverse ladder opponents on Kaggle.
Each evaluation game takes roughly 0.3-0.6 seconds CPU; total per-node evaluation must stay well within the execution timeout, bounding how many games and policy variants can be measured per node.
The agent must NEVER raise an exception during a game (an exception forfeits the game); all policy code must be wrapped with a safe fallback returning the first maxCount legal option indices.
Hidden information (opponent hand, both prize contents, deck order) is not visible in observations; only opponent board, counts, and logs are available, limiting the accuracy of any lookahead.
